title: The Buddha Lies Down
hook: a late night of teaching, an aching back, and the Buddha lying down in the middle of it
carry: the lion's posture: rest inside the work, then rise
tomorrow: an old man, sick and tired. what line sent him home glowing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a teacher on frosty leaves who slept well, because the fevers of the mind had cooled. Sleep well. Today, the rest that comes in the middle of the work.

A nap at four in the afternoon can feel like a confession: I quit early, I'm lazy, everyone else is still going. Now a hall, newly built, full of people who have come to hear the Buddha. He has been teaching them deep into the night. The lamps are burning, the crowd is still listening, and the Buddha turns to his attendant Ananda and says: my back is aching. I'm going to stretch it. In front of everyone, in the middle of the evening, the teacher lies down.
screen: `A NAP THAT FEELS LIKE QUITTING.` → `A FULL HALL, DEEP IN THE NIGHT.` → `MY BACK ACHES. I'LL LIE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Watch how he does it, because the sutta takes care to tell us. Before he lies down he asks Ananda to teach the gathering in his place, so the work goes on. Then he folds his robe, lies on his right side in what the texts call the lion's posture, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clearly aware, with the thought of getting up again in mind. Ananda teaches the path of one in training. And when he's done, the Buddha gets up and tells him: good, Ananda, good. That small scene holds a lot. The Buddha doesn't apologize for his back. He doesn't push through until he collapses, and he doesn't drop the whole evening either. He rests inside the work, on purpose, and he trusts someone else to carry it for a while. That's the difference between rest and quitting. Quitting walks away from the work. Rest stays near it, lies down mindfully, and keeps the thought of rising. The Buddhist path names right effort as one of its eight parts, and right effort, in this picture, includes a body that gets to stop. Even a teacher whose whole life was effort lay down when his back ached. Here's a detail to tell someone tonight: in the suttas, the lion's posture is how the Buddha lies down to rest, mindful, with the intention to rise.
screen: `ANANDA TEACHES IN HIS PLACE.` · `THE LION'S POSTURE.` · `REST STAYS NEAR THE WORK.` · `THE THOUGHT OF RISING.` · then, large: `REST.`

segments.voice: Sit back, or lie down if you can, and let the shoulders drop. Let the hands rest open, the belly soften and the jaw go loose, the way the Buddha let his back stretch out. Rest on purpose, without guilt, knowing you will get up again when the sit ends.
Rest: lying down mindfully inside the work, with the intention to rise, as the Buddha did when his back ached.
One line to keep: the lion's posture. Rest inside the work, mindful, with the thought of rising. Two of nine.

screen: `DAY 1618 COUNTS.` → `BODY, ILLNESS AND AGE · 2 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT LINE SENT A SICK OLD MAN HOME GLOWING?`

howItsDone: Monastics in many Buddhist traditions are taught to lie down mindfully in the lion's posture, on the right side, noting the intention to rise; lay practitioners sometimes use the same posture for rest.

what a scholar hears: MN 53 (Sekha Sutta) sets the scene at the new assembly hall of the Sakyans in Kapilavatthu; the lion's posture with mindfulness and the perception of rising recurs in the suttas.

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's cousin and longtime attendant

lion's posture.meaning: lying on the right side, mindful, one foot resting on the other

right effort.meaning: one of the eight parts of the Buddhist path

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 53 (Sekha Sutta: after teaching the Sakyans late into the night, the Buddha says his back is uncomfortable, asks Ananda to teach, and lies down in the lion's posture, mindful, noting the time to rise; afterward he approves Ananda's teaching)

notes: Story shape: the scene (the Buddha lies down mid-evening) is the hook's cliffhanger; the teach tells how and why.

MN 53 paraphrased. Confirm: the hall is newly built by the Sakyans; the Buddha taught 'much of the night'; he folds his outer robe and lies in the lion's posture 'with the perception of rising'. 'Lamps burning' is a light scene-setting touch; cut if a Keeper prefers.
'Right effort as one of its eight parts' refers to the Noble Eightfold Path; 'a body that gets to stop' is an interpretive line from this scene, not a quotation.
